utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Since this is the first hearing of this year, I would like to express our expectation that we will have a good successful co-operation and a fair and expeditious trial ahead. I wish everybody health and a good work. Before the next witness will be brought in, I would like to raise briefly four matters. The first is dealing with documents marked for identification in relation to the decision, 92 bis. On the 27th of January 2011, the Chamber received a list from the Registry assigning exhibit numbers to all documents of pure, that means without cross-examination, 92 bis Prosecution witnesses currently marked for identification. The Chamber hereby admits the listed documents into evidence, and asks the Registry to proceed accordingly. The Chamber has been informed by the Registry that an international -- that an internal memorandum assigning exhibit numbers to these documents will be filed within the next couple of days. The second matter deals with documents marked for identification pending translation. The Chamber has received some information, some days ago, about some Prosecution documents which have now their translation. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. It's good to be back and I have the exhibit numbers of these materials that have now been uploaded and I can read them so we get them in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These documents are now in evidence in this trial. Mr. Tolimir and the Defence, the same duty is for the Defence. Do you have an update, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. First of all, good afternoon to everyone. The translations of the following exhibits marked for identification have been uploaded: D132, D106, D103, D97, D95, D93, and D91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These documents will be admitted documents as well. Now I would like to turn to another topic. Just before the winter recess, an important and time-sensitive filing was, for various reasons, misplaced and not filed in the case record as it should have been. As a result, the Chamber did not receive the filing in a timely manner. The Chamber takes this opportunity to remind the parties, and in particular the Defence, and those assisting us in the courtroom, that there is a well-known and long-standing procedure at this Tribunal for the filing of documents. Such filings should not be left to chance but should be submitted and received properly and with the utmost attention. The fourth and last point -- I refer now to the notice of witness scheduling and time estimates for direct and cross-examination. I note that paragraph 1 of the annex to the order concerning guidelines on the presentation of evidence and conduct of the parties during trial, issued on the 24th of February 2010, directs the calling party to file, by the 15th of each month, a list of witnesses scheduled for the following calendar month and time estimates for the examination of each witness. The cross-examining party is required to file its estimated length for cross-examination of those witnesses within seven days of that filing. This month, the Prosecution filed its notice on the 17th of January, which is fine in light of the holidays. However, the Chamber did not receive from the accused his time estimates for the cross-examination of these witnesses until the 30th of January 2010, that is yesterday. The timely receipt of these estimates is necessary for the organisation of the witness schedule and to ensure that court time is used in the most efficient manner possible. It is essential that the accused file its notices on time each month. The Chamber would like -- also like to address the filing of weekly notices of witness schedules and time estimates. The second paragraph of the annex of the order I just mentioned, the calling party is directed to provide its weekly schedule of witnesses a week before the week in which those witnesses are expected to testify. However, the Chamber has become aware that the current practice in place has not abided by this rule. Therefore, the Chamber proposes to alter the direction such that the Prosecution would be required to file its weekly witness notice by 4 p.m. on the Thursday before the week the witnesses will testify, and the accused to provide his time estimate for cross-examination of each of those witnesses the day -- the next day, that means by Friday, 4 p.m. Are there any submissions by the parties in this respect? I don't see any. Then an amendment of the said order reflecting this new guideline will be filed shortly. Now I don't see any other matters to be raised before the witness is being brought in. Please, the witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome to the Tribunal. We are very glad that you were able to come to The Hague. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey is examining you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And as the Court will recall, Dr. Haglund is a 92 bis witness so this shouldn't -- this will be an abbreviated direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us your name and spell your last name?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: William Dale Haglund, H-a-g-l-u-n-d.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'm a forensic anthropologist and death investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you received a Ph.D. in that field?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we all know that you've had some tough issues with your heart and we weren't sure if we were going to be able to get you here. We're glad to see you as the President said. How are you feeling? Are you going to be up for this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I feel fine and I'm happy to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just let us know if there is anything we should know about. Have you had a chance to look at your testimony in the Popovic and the Krstic cases?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you and I discuss an error that I will point out, it was on -- in the Popovic case, page 8905 of 15 March 2007, that should come up on the screen, but I think in a question early on by myself, it is said, on page 12, and I'll wait a bit so you can see this, line 12 and 13, I'll just read it and if it comes up, it comes up, it's not crucial. I think we've got it there. There we go. I asked you on line 12, okay, and you've, I believe, described yourself as a forensic pathologist? Now --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No. I know I'm not a pathologist. I wouldn't have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So we can change that to as you have what have -- you have just said, anthropologist, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I think I see that in other places in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind both speakers to pause between question and answer because you are using the same language and we need interpretation to different other languages, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And perhaps it was my mistake, but I'm not sure I've ever made a mistake, so perhaps not, but so if you were asked the same questions you were asked in those previous trials, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. President, I have a memorandum from the court officer dated 3 November 2010, and it has -- it's a fairly extensive list of reports, exhibits, testimonies from both his previous trials, which are basically the basis for the 92 bis testimony. And we've reviewed it and it is correct, and you'll see the last page of that, there are some of his reports, there are four exhibits that came in for whatever reason, they were shown to other expert witnesses and are already in evidence, so if we could just take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. I have to interrupt you. I was quite concerned about this list. Last week in preparation of this trial today, they were marked for identification with the witness Dusan Janc but were not tendered at that point in time, these three forensic investigation reports of witness Haglund. But the numbers are correct. They are marked for identification up to now. Just to clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was concerned about them also, and I apologise for that wrong information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My microphone was not activated. I have to repeat that. They were tendered through expert witness Baraybar, not Dusan Janc. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart informs me that according to her e-court -- you are correct now. So that was initially our mistake and so we would offer all these materials, I don't think there is any dispute, into evidence pursuant to the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first one is the testimony in Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the first page of this memo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. And this is P1306 MFI'd. Before we make a decision, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I recall that not all the documents that are being admitted through this witness have been translated into a language that the accused understands; i.e., we don't have the Serbian translation. Some of the documents are affected and the list clearly indicates which of the documents have translations and which do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And which list do you find such an indication that there is no translation yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have before us the list normally sent by the OTP to the Registry and the parties, Prosecution Exhibits for witness number 11, and the ERN numbers we will see that in some of the documents lack translations; for instance, the document under 65 ter number 6649 does not have a Serbian translation. This is just an illustration. As does not 6651, then 6652. Next, 65 ter 6648.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understood what you are referring to in the Prosecution exhibits list, in the column with the ERN numbers we have always in brackets the addition ENG, that means English, and sometimes B/C/S T, for instance, 65 ter 00577 has such a comment. I would like to ask you, Mr. McCloskey, does that mean these have a B/C/S translation and the others indicated as ENG have no translation yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is basically correct. And let me explain. The first five exhibits underneath that second heading, you'll notice in the far right-hand column they all have D numbers and these were bits and pieces of articles that were all used by the Defence in the cross-examination of Dr. Haglund that, for completeness, we wanted to offer as exhibits. Ms. Stewart has asked those to be translated so we hope to get those back. And the other material, and I do want to respond to you that Mr. Gajic and I do have very good communication, we have consulted and discussed with each other on a number of topics over the break, and I think he would agree with me we have very good communication, I don't recall that we have discussed this particular translation issue. But when we see all of these reports by Dr. Haglund, the body of the report, where he is making his conclusions, that material is translated. It's been translated for years. But Dr. Haglund, who started out in this field in 1996, he, unlike some of the other experts, attached indexes and lists as well as autopsy reports to his report so that when we offer in Dr. Haglund's report all this supporting material to it comes with it; whereas, the other -- many of the -- and if not all of the other experts identified all that material and it's been provided to the Defence but it's not been part of the record because it doesn't normally help us much in the trial, in the courtroom. So we have never sent that material for translation, much of it's untranslatable in any realistic sense because it's nothing but lists, long list us of ligatures and artifacts and things like that. The other documents that he attached, he attached all the autopsy reports that the forensic pathologists used as well, and so we have many, many of those reports that we have never sent for translation, just they are so voluminous and there has never been any specific reason for us to do that. Nor have I ever heard, as far as I can recall, any specific request on the part of any Defence over the years, so I'm not aware of their concern in that because it would -- it would be a real burden for CLSS to translate this. Now, if there are particular areas or autopsy reports that the Defence is concerned with, we will of course join them and get them to CLSS, but Dr. Haglund is not a forensic pathologist, though he, as you heard before, as an anthropologist, his -- he worked with the pathologists in the morgue to help them but he -- to assist everyone initially he attached those to his record. No other autopsy reports of John Clark and the other pathologists have ever been translated and I don't recall there being a problem when Dr. Clark came in, so I would -- I may be mistaken but we are ready to work with the Defence on that, but it's just one of those things that I don't really think is necessary but I would like to hear from Mr. Gajic on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's hear Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, presumably both the Chamber and the OTP are aware of the fact that Mr. Tolimir does not speak English. Under our 94 bis filing, I don't recall the date of the filing, we drew your attention to the problem of translation, i.e., that not all the documents have their respective translations. This was a long time ago, and ahead of Mr. Tolimir's cross-examination of any witness, Mr. Tolimir needs to have the Serbian text of all the documents before him. It is at times difficult for the Defence to have such voluminous documents translated itself through its own resources, due to the fact that some of the translations are lacking or are taking a long time to be made. As for the first five documents on the list here, they are very important documents. It is true that they were admitted as Defence exhibits in other cases. However, this witness appears here under 92 ter. In other words, under the rules all the documentation admitted pursuant to this rule has to have respective translations. Equally so, whenever the Defence wishes to have documents admitted that exist only in the Serbian version they are marked for identification until they receive their translation. And lastly, of course, Mr. Tolimir would very much like to have documents admitted into evidence which he can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I suggest to proceed in the following way. First we receive the transcript in the Popovic case, 65 ter 6647 as an exhibit under the P number 1306. All the other documents listed in the list of the Prosecution will be admitted, some of them marked for identification pending translation. I will not read them out into the record. Everybody knows which is only in English and which is already translated. The Chamber would invite the parties to contact and discuss the matter and to look into the documents, which of them are really necessary to be translated for a fair trial, and in which cases there is no need for that. And then we -- both parties should come back to the Chamber at a later stage. Not to save more time of the examination of the witness, Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sure we'll work something out on that. So I will take a moment to read a summary of Dr. Haglund and then some short, hopefully very brief, questions. Dr. Haglund is a forensic anthropologist from the United States. He has been conducting forensic investigations since 1993. In addition to his extensive domestic experience, he has worked internationally, including work for the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in East Timor, Somaliland, Afghanistan, and Iraq. Dr. Haglund also worked for the ICTR in 1996 and was involved significantly in those -- some of those investigation exhumations. He also began work for the ICTY in 1996 through middle of 1998 when he finished his final reports. He was the senior forensic consultant for the OTP at that time. As senior forensic consultant in 1996, Dr. Haglund led a team in the excavation and exhumation of several mass graves associated with the fall of Srebrenica, including the graves at Cerska, Nova Kasaba, Lazete which we know to be the area of Orahovac, and Pilica. While Dr. Haglund himself is not an archaeologist, he had archeologists on his exhumation team working with him and advising him. After exhuming human remains from graves, forensic anthropologists, together with forensic pathologists, worked at the morgue and examined and, when necessary, reconstructed victims' remains so as to determine their sex and age as well as the minimum number of individuals contained in each grave, by examining their bones. Dr. Haglund and the forensic anthropologists also helped pathologists identify injuries to skeletal remains, though Dr. Haglund did not spend a lot of time at the morgue. Dr. Haglund prepared reports setting out his team's findings in respect of each of the grave sites and he enclosed the autopsy reports of the forensic pathologists and many of the indexes to his reports. During the course of their work, Dr. Haglund and his team also documented items, including ligatures and blindfolds that they found with the bodies in the graves. For instance, of the 33 victims found at the Nova Kasaba grave sites, 27 of them had bindings around their arms. Some of these victims were still in the kneeling position with their torsos and heads bent forward and their hands tied behind their backs. The vast majority of those victims at Nova Kasaba found in this position had suffered gunshot wounds to the head. In the Pilica grave, Dr. Haglund and his team recovered a minimum of 132 individuals. In the Cerska grave, Dr. Haglund and his team recovered 150 individuals. Back in 1996, there were some complaints against Dr. Haglund by some of his colleagues in relation to his work on the Srebrenica-related mass graves. The allegations were investigated by a panel of experts whose findings are set out in the San Antonio oversight committee report. Of the 17 professionals involved in the work with Dr. Haglund and interviewed by the panel, 14 professionals were favourable to Dr. Haglund and four had some complaints. One of the criticisms was that Dr. Haglund worked too fast and brought too many bodies out of the grave in one day. The panel reviewed these complaints and did not find any evidence of wrong doing by Dr. Haglund or anything that he did or his team did that jeopardised the scientific validity of his findings. However, the panel did find that the forensic pathologists overseeing the work at the morgue acted inappropriately when, in some cases, he changed the cause of death in autopsy reports without consulting the pathologist who had conducted the original autopsy. Dr. Haglund was aware of the process that the OTP went through where it went around the world and provided all of the original reports of the -- to the original pathologists for their review and for their final conclusion on the cause of death. Dr. Haglund testified as an expert in several ICTR cases, including the case of the Prosecutor versus Georges Rutaganda. In the final judgement of that case, the Trial Chamber set aside part of the conclusions of Dr. Haglund based on their analysis of the testimony of the Defence expert on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Haglund, is there -- as you will recall we went over those complaints in much more detail in your last testimony. Is there anything regarding any of what I have read, especially those complaints, that you want to add at this time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so let me just take us very briefly, Pilica. The Trial Chamber has been to the area where you were working. Can you just describe briefly so they can get an idea of what was the size of that grave, as you -- as you exhumed it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The depression that -- indicated the grave was at 28 metres long and 6 metres, I think 6 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall roughly how deep it was at its deepest point?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: At the deepest point it was nearly 3 metres deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you find any bodies in that hole?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, at the extreme end of the grave, there were -- there was a pile of an assemblage of remains, 132 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And Cerska, were you the first one to really arrive and do a full exhumation of the Cerska grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just -- just very briefly, describe to the Court what you did and what you found on that grave, just so they can get a little feeling of it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Do you want me to describe the situation there and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you got there, just as best you can recollect, and then just the size, the number of bodies?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The Cerska grave was on a gravelled road, going up a little mountain area to the village of Cerska. The grave was at the side of the road where an embankment, when they did the road they made a cut in the road so that there was a steep area where earth had been removed to put the road in, and then the continuing slope on the other side. There was a gaping hole where soil and gravel had been removed from that cut, and the bodies and the -- there were clusters of ammunition on that side of the grave. On the other side of the grave, overlooking the slope, it became evident that the killers had stood on the far side of the grave, that the individuals that were being killed were lined up alongside the grave and were shot from where the gravel had been taken place across the way. They had been lined up, we saw clusters of cartridge casings that were ejected from automatic weapons as the guns had been fired, and then the people that had been shot had been -- had fallen over the edge or were rolled over the edge, and then at that time the gravel was moved by machine and then the bodies were covered up on that slope, about six metres down and about 30 metres long, they were spread out along lines apparently when they were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us -- you made some conclusions there. Can you tell us before you go any further what are you basing your conclusion on that it was, for example, this soil or this dirt was moved by machines over the top of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They had had the gouge in that area in order to remove that, it had to reach high and they wouldn't have been able to do it by shovel. They had to do it by machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you also concluded that the victims were shot. Can you -- do you have any -- any factors that led you to this conclusion that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, certainly the cartridge casings that were clustered in various clusters on the far side of the road, and when the gravel and the -- and the fill, to cover up the remains, was removed, some of those cartridge casings were also and included in the fill of the grave when they covered the bodies. And then the pathologists determined from the angles of shots, they knew that the shooters were lined up in a row, they came to that conclusion, and they saw different directions of shots for individuals. Individuals standing in one place would sort of in a spray type, as it was, motion were shooting at the individuals, with somebody from another position be shooting at them from another angle and so they would have different angles in the shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the remains themselves? Did you find any -- any evidence in the grave -- in and around the remains that gave you any indications of execution?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, the -- of the 149, there were gunshot wounds, there were 48 ligatures found in the grave. Some of them associated with the remains, but -- and some of them on the remains actually them self, the hands or arms were bound behind the backs, mostly with wire ligatures. And these individuals were not in one place but they were found amongst other bodies that didn't have ligatures in the same -- in the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us whether you were able to determine whether this was a primary undisturbed grave or whether this grave had been disturbed? These are terms that this Court is of course at this point very well familiar with.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was a primary undisturbed grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Pilica? Were you able to make a determination on that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was a bit more complex. The grave for the most part of it -- a very large grave, only on one end of the grave, the far end of the grave, from where the digging had been started to make a ramp down into the grave, there was only that one pile with some of -- disassociated remains that were recovered from a couple other places but most of them intermingled with the pile of individuals there. And amongst the pile there was also a vegetation that was consistent with the vegetation that was by the road coming in from the farm and to the area of the grave, and that could have been caused by the bodies shot in the field and maybe a front end loader or machine like that would scrape up the bodies. As they scraped up the bodies, they would picked up portions of sod and grasses from the area where the individuals were shot, and as they picked them up in that way, then the pushing bodies with the front end loader to get this expanse of bodies picked up, they would be cutting some of them in pieces and separating some of the body parts. And so when these were in the grave, we found pieces of sod, we found some disarticulated bodies, some bodies that were still complete, et cetera, mixed up in one pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you -- were you able to form a conclusion whether or not that Pilica had been disturbed in the sense that had it -- you saw other graves?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, having been moved into the grave, to me it wasn't that as clear as the Lazete grave, and maybe a lot of the soil itself that would have been contaminated by human bodies decomposing and leaking into the substrate, we didn't find that, only in the area where the pile of bodies was, the assemblage of the victims. That doesn't mean it was not disturbed, but I didn't have the information that would allow me to -- to say that concretely. It seemed more consistent to me at that time that the disarticulation, et cetera, was -- was due to the bodies being placed in the field and then scraped up by machine, but that was still an open thing. I didn't feel I should -- I would just wait and see what happened with other exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you ever have a chance in those early days of 1996 to take part in any exhumations of secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No. No. I had no -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you mention that Lazete in your view was a secondary -- was disturbed and the Trial Chamber has heard quite a bit of evidence on it, you've testified previously on that so I won't go into that, but I do want to ask you about one thing. The Trial Chamber has heard from a forensic -- I believe he was an archaeologist that I'm sure you know, Fredy Peccerelli?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And his exhumation of a grave at Lazete, the one that is closest to the railroad tracks?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it was referred to you as Lazete 2B. Can you tell us, did you -- did you exhume Lazete 2B in 1996?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you get all the bodies out of it, as far as you knew when you were there doing it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that at least one individual was there. It was a time -- indeed, if you recall, that was a big long trench where bodies were dumped in separate piles, and the part -- at the time it was a very torrential rainy season, the grave was about three metres deep, the sides of the grave were collapsing, and it was a danger to the workers in the field and I determined that we should stop the exhumation at that time. People would know there were remains in there, recorded that, and that it could be returned to at some other future time when the weather wasn't as dangerous for security of the individuals working in the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And one last topic that I think you perhaps -- you're perhaps one of the only people that can really talk about, and that is the security situation on the ground in 1996. We are more familiar with the situation as it is today, but can you tell us what kind of security threat, if there was one, what kind of security you had, just give us a feel for what -- what you were up against in those days, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In the area where the -- of the Tuzla area of where the autopsies were performed, it was relatively safe. The scientists could drive their vehicles to and from Tuzla to where the examination area was. It was next to a military base also. In the Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. When you say military base, which military?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was a -- what they called it then, it was an American military base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it was NATO?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was a NATO base, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In the Republika Srpska, the workers were -- had to stay at a NATO base, and when we -- nobody drove -- they were not allowed to drive alone anywhere. They -- in the mornings, before the team went to the scenes, Bradleys were sent to the scene -- the team to, for instance in Cerska, to guard the road entering into the road up to the village of Cerska and alongside which was the Cerska grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say Bradleys, again --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: These are small tanks, small -- various -- well, small, small military tanks. And then when the -- the workers were taken and the scientists were taken to the grave site. They went in a convoy with two Humvee vehicles in front with 55 calibre machine-guns and two of them in the back and that's the only way they could travel to get to and from the gives, and the soldiers would stay all day to guard the graves, and -- however, there was a problem with the security, and there was a mention in the -- what -- can I remember the -- oh, I'll remember in a second. But there was a problem, according to the Dayton agreement, excuse me, of the -- NATO did not have to guard the graves. They had many, many other priorities, they didn't have the resources to set people on grave, to guard the graves, but the Dayton agreement said that they needed to protect the workers for ICTY, working on the graves. So the first evening we -- they had -- of the ICTY had hired some guards on the grave in the morning and that was just the first day we were there and we were -- the dogs were going through and do -- we had to do ordnance. Looking for ordnance, we wouldn't put anybody on a grave until we'd -- we were using dog teams for the most part and they would go through very efficiently through the grave to see if there was any unexploded ordnance. That was completed the first day, with -- initial mapping and the grave was not open, but the individuals that had been left at the grave were not there in the morning. They had been threatened by a local population and they got afraid and they left. So the second day, towards the afternoon, when our workers and myself would have to go back to the army base, I refused to leave the grave, and I was told that there were many correspondences between Brussels and between the NATO leaders of the military -- of NATO command, the -- where we were staying at the military base, and they finally decided that they would leave soldiers there to guard us throughout the night, and so myself, John Gerns, and Jose Pablo who were ICTY employees, two of us would stay there every night through the time that we did that grave and we were guarded by NATO troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get any visible air support in any way?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. In the initial time we would have Harrier flyovers at various times during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have any assurance from day to day whether you would be able to actually go back to the -- to the grave to conduct your work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No. It was a pretty uncertain time because there would be incidents in the Republika Srpska that made travelling in that not as easy, and the military would concentrate on those areas and they didn't have -- wouldn't have had time to deal with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Haglund. I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. I have to come back, I'm sorry for that, to the documents we have admitted into evidence or marked for identification, that was only related to the documents starting with P1307 through P1334. Then in the memorandum of the Registry we have four additional documents with some problems, the first of them, the first three of them, are part of your list you provided the Chamber with. The first P number is wrong. It should read P1071 instead of 1017. That is also received like the two additional ones, 1072 and 1073. Then there is listed P01221, and that is in effect the same as the document P1359 in the next internal memorandum of the Registry of the 12th of November 2010. This document has two different numbers but is the same. That should be figured out and the Registry should remove one of them, if I am not mistaken. In your list, there is P13 -- no, sorry. You have listed the 65 ter number 06653. That is not admitted into evidence at the moment because you didn't use it with this witness, and it was not used in the prior trial. I hope I was able to make it clear, this is P1360 MFI. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. The memo I had didn't have that last one on it, but I thank you for clarifying that. The other internal memo you referred to that -- apparently there is a list of the Krstic testimony twice, we didn't get internal memo but I thank you for correcting that and we just need that Krstic testimony in only once. And I thank the Court's efforts for sorting this out, and we will continue to make sure that we sort this out so that you're not having to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You didn't use the document P01360. This is an article titled, "Scientists Quest for Justice" with this witness. This is not admitted yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we don't need that. Leave that where it is, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies the situation. Mr. Tolimir, now it is time for your cross-examination. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to greet everybody. May peace be unto this house and may this day in court and the final judgement reflect God's will and not my will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to great Dr. Haglund, welcome here, and also I wish you a safe journey home once this is over. I would like to start from the last issue that you mentioned. You said that in certain situation you needed air support and also on land you needed guards to guard you while you were working. Could you tell me exactly on which location these measures were necessary?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The planes, I had nothing to do with. The military did that. But that was only at the Cerska grave that I'm aware of that happened. On all other graves, we had the accompaniment of a NATO contingent for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us why were these guards necessary in Cerska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, as I think it's demonstrated that the first guards at the first grave the first night we were working in the field, they were of -- by local residents, they were threatened by local residents enough to scare them away from being at the grave site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the fact that in Cerska, there is no other population except Muslims? That place where you worked, did you notice any Muslim settlements or Serb settlements there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: We never stopped at any of those settlements. We just drove straight to the grave, so I'm not familiar with what groups were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. However, just a minute ago you said that the guards were attacked while guarding the place. So if there was no local population there, who else could have attacked them in your estimate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I never said that they were attacked. I said they were threatened. How that happened, I do not know. They were not there but they had informed some of the military, before they left, that they had been threatened, they were leaving. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, did you speak to any of those individuals who declared that they had been threatened in Cerska, and do you know exactly who made those threats and in which way?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, page 20, line 24, you said that the International Tribunal hired some people to act as guards. Do you remember that you said that a moment ago during the direct examination?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They hired some people to guard the grave in the evenings, yes, and then subsequently, they used their own people to guard the graves in the evenings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So those guards were there, why exactly? Because they hired them or because there was a real need to have guards at the locality where you worked?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It's absolutely, it's -- it has to do with the chain of custody and the chain of evidence. Once a grave is opened, then it's liable to be interfered with, at least that's always a problem with the Court and the Defence, they are going to attack you if you have not been in charge of that grave in one way or secured that grave for the complete time that you've been there working, and that was necessary. Otherwise your evidence would not stand up in at least in American courts I know, and I sort of went towards the -- that -- the ideas that I have learned and had utilised in the United States, and so they have to have somebody there at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you said that you left one grave site. Can you tell us where was it? You mentioned that you left the grave because of the weather conditions, so can you tell us was that particular grave site under guard until you returned?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The grave was covered up again with drive-bys by the military and we could have told if it was at some times -- it wasn't until two years that that grave was -- the other remains were removed. At the time I was there, we collected information that you'll see in the reports, but we -- we left the remains in there at the bottom of that grave, at least the one that we knew was there, because it was just too dangerous for people to work in the grave. If I might clarify, I'm sorry, but the grave did receive those drive-by looks at the grave to see if it had been disturbed, but the subsequent exhumation of the grave showed that the archeologists did not see any disturbance of how -- from the time that since we had left the grave the way it was. When they removed the remains, they saw the same things that we did in the bottom of the grave and they -- when they found that one individual and they found some others beside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that it was only an assumption that there could be a threat to the people who worked on the graves, or was there a real danger as a cause to engage both NATO and air support and all these things that you mentioned? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was the -- in respect to the chain of custody that we had to guard the grave as we were working on it. As far as the protection and ensurance of security for the teams, that was a NATO decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, was it very expensive to pay for all these forces giving all this security, protecting the crew that was performing the expert work on the locality? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That -- they did that work, I have no idea how expensive it was. I imagine it cost them, but they didn't let it interfere with their duties at the -- other duties they had to do; for instance, when there was an election, I believe, at that time they asked us to not work those days so that they could use their troops to make sure that the election went along in a satisfactory and peaceful manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us which year, which period?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: This is 1996, would have been from -- it was -- we were there from July through late August or September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 13, during the direct examination, Mr. McCloskey said that the pathologist changed the cause of death and you confirmed it. Can you elaborate on this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I wasn't aware there was a change until I was told that, and that was after the exhumations pretty much were finished. That was only the director of the -- representing the Physicians for Human Rights. His changes were made. The changes that he made were -- many pathologists come from different areas and they would -- the cause of death was different. Some of them would say there are five gunshot wounds to the head, and other people would say it's multiple gunshot wounds that caused the deaths, and I think what Dr. Kirschner was trying to do was saying in order for putting these things, reports and stuff together, to say multiple gunshot wounds, his problem was that he didn't apparently talk to some of the pathologists and that was -- that was changing their reports and that was not a proper thing to do. I was not involved with that, so ... I was not aware that it was going on, and it wasn't my place because Dr. Kirschner was officially in charge of the autopsy procedures, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, you mentioned the Medecins Sans Frontieres or Physicians for Human Rights. So can you tell us what were they doing there and what was their role during exhumations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The Physicians for Human Rights was asked by Dr. Goldstone because of their experience internationally in doing this kind of work and humanitarian work and identifying individuals, if they could put together a team of volunteers, they were not paid. They got a little, minor subsistence allowance, and so they, and basically I knew most of the people that were working in the area and I picked out the people that came, and what they did so as much a volunteer because they weren't really being paid. When ICTY started sending people in, and then they started paying them wages. And I'm not sure I clarified the -- an answer to your question. I think I've forgotten part of it, but they were there at the behest of the Tribunal, essentially, because it was known that they were probably the best group to do something like that because they had experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you mention this, can you also tell us who was the founder of this organisation, Physicians for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was a group of physicians from, I believe in Boston, I'm not too sure who founded, the individual that founded it. You would be able to find out on their website, I'm sure, but I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us who would pay the subsistence to those volunteers during which period and from which source?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'm not aware of their financial things, but they were given money by various human rights groups and the -- they got some money from a group in Belgium, I know, and various other contributions. They -- they survive on contributions and getting grants for particular projects and that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So besides this financing, can you also tell us, did they have any formal or informal connections with official institutions of the United States, since you told us that their headquarters was in Boston.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Do you mean with government organisations? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. That's what I said. Both official and unofficial institutions there.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Of -- they did not deal with government institutions. Moneys that came to that project for the exhumations came from non-governmental entities, not from the government. That was very explicit in their charter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also tell us whether the majority of similar organisations is financed in the same way, that is from the non-governmental sector, and then they also receive some donations, and you certainly, as an American, have some personal experience about it, could you also tell us what is the way in which they procure their financing? And does that mean that they were better paid than you people working for the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the financial connection that the groups like the Argentinians and the Guatemalans have, I have no idea. I'm aware of the individuals that have worked with me, but I'm not aware of their -- their financial arrangements and that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, you said that they were invited by a certain physician or more precisely, Dr. Goldstone. I don't want to make any mistakes about it, but I want to ask you the following: If he invited them, how could it be that they performed the exhumation of mass graves? That's a job where only experts should be engaged in, experts who can be responsible for the job that they do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Dr. Goldstone asked the Physicians for Human Rights to pick out the team. He did not pick out team members. And we had worked with human rights groups throughout the world and the most experienced at that time for skeletal remains in mass graves -- because we don't have many mass graves in the United States, we had individuals from I think at least 15 different countries. We tried to pick out the experts that we thought were most -- most useful. We had one Argentinian, I think three Guatemalans, I had somebody from Peru, various human rights groups, and those human rights groups really didn't have a great deal to do with the governments. That's what they were -- they were doing -- they were doing work that the government -- they were doing remains and recovering remains and trying to identify them that the government, the previous government, had killed, so they didn't have a really good relationship with the government. They weren't -- I don't think they were getting money at that time from governments. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who is this Dr. Goldstone that you mentioned? And what was his role in relation to you and the teams that performed their work there, that performed exhumations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, he was the -- in charge of ICTY, as far as investigations go. He was a Supreme Court judge from South Africa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he impose the teams on you, Mr. Goldstone and the International Tribunal, or did you have a free hand to choose them according to their competence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: When I take -- undertake a job, then basically no one tells me who I can hire and what kind of expertise I need and what I need to do. I know what to do. No, I had no -- no prodding, no -- from anybody, in choosing the teams, no interference by the Tribunal at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have now in e-court P1071? It is one of the reports -- it says on the front page, Dr. William Haglund, senior forensic adviser of the ICTY and the organisation Physicians for Human Rights. Thank you. Okay. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the following, if you can give us your answer. When in this report you mention organisations for human rights, can you tell us, during the exhumations in Bosnia that you took part in, which function did you have within Physicians for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I work with the Tribunal not for Physicians for Human Rights. I had done some work for them prior to 1996, but I was an employee of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And how much time had elapsed between your working for them and in Bosnia? And what were the locations that you worked on?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Mostly Honduras.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on, when you finished exhumations in Bosnia, did you have any connections with the Physicians for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: From -- I recall when I first started. From mid-1998 through, I think, 2000, I was the director of their international forensic investigation department.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So can we say, then, that you knew them well, both before you worked in Bosnia and after, when you continued your work with them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I can see here, in the report, that you were senior forensic adviser of the Tribunal. So my question is: Were you the senior forensic adviser of the Tribunal or of the OTP of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Senior forensic adviser.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us were you senior forensic adviser of the Tribunal or of the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I was -- I would presume that I work with the Prosecutor's Office for that. That's who I related to for the most, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So can I then say that you were an adviser of the Prosecutor's Office based on your answer? Or should I question you further on in this regard?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In regards to the exhumation, yes, I was the adviser, for the -- for the exhumation work on the team that I led.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, can you then tell us who was your immediate superior, which person or body from which you received your tasks? For instance, where you had to go, what you had to do and similar things.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In 1995, I did assessments for both Rwanda and for -- for ICTY. At that time, in Rwanda, I assessed graves to see what they were like, how kinds of -- you know, there were latrines, there were caves, there were buried remains, remains on the surfaces, remains in latrines, and I had to go through and pick out graves that had not been disturbed that would have the most evidence, and then I gave them a listing of those, and based on the trials that they were prepared to proceed on, that was how the decision would be made. I would suggest what I thought would be the best grave, and usually they would accept that and that's how they were chosen. In 1995, when I finished in Rwanda, I was asked to come by the ICTY, and if I would do some assessments for them. And I did that at that time also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understood that. My question, however, was: Who gave you the tasks? Who told you what to do in the localities, such as Cerska, Lazete, and other places?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, the protocols for autopsy were written by the -- Dr. Kirschner, and the protocols for the exhumation, et cetera, those were -- those were from me, and the examination of skeletons, that came from me. I wasn't told by anybody what we needed to do to complete an exhumation or the examination of remains. I was familiar with those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would that be a convenient time for our first break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haglund, we must have our first break now and we will resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, we stopped just as I was about to ask you who it was who gave you tasks as to which locations you should attend. So first of all, who gave you the task to go to Bosnia and specifically to Cerska, et cetera? Or was it a matter of your own choice? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was a matter of being requested to do it. It was my choice to do so. I'd like to clarify one thing, if I may, from our last part of the testimony. I sat down in the waiting room and I felt like maybe I was acting as a dictator or something, but I had a wonderful group of people, some experts had more expertise in certain areas than I did, and I'd work with many of them and I trusted them very well. And as well, ICTY. And I had not worked with lot with them, but the people that worked for me, they had had good suggestions and they had information that I didn't have and I listened to them. It's just that I was -- you probably have been in the same position, you have to make the final decision, but we are dependent upon the great workers we work with and the information they'd have often times to help us make our decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haglund. Please tell us, before leaving for Bosnia, did you come to the Tribunal here and, if so, who did you meet with and who told you what your tasks in Bosnia would be? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I came to the Tribunal before I went to Rwanda, because of the -- the head of the -- Dr. Goldstone was actually in charge of Rwanda as well as ICTY, as far as the investigations were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that before leaving for the former Yugoslavia, you first got in touch with Dr. Goldstone?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I came to the -- here to talk to the -- the only -- the head investigator -- for the head investigator for -- but this individual was the head for two organisations -- for Rwanda, and I don't know if it was here but he was staying here, not in Rwanda at the time. So I was -- it was interesting -- and I needed to come and be more familiar with the situation down there and of what I might expect as far as living, et cetera, and that, and who I needed to speak to in Kigali, Rwanda, the capital, where the investigation unit was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the name of this head investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Off-hand, do I not recall it, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, tell us, had you known the head of investigations from before, and did you know what his authority was and what his duties were, since he was in that other place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'd never met him before, but he was involved with investigations going on in Rwanda. I never saw him in Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you meet him in the former Yugoslavia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you contact him at any point after your departure from Rwanda? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No. By then I think they had a separate investigation head in Rwanda and in ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On your arrival in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, who received you and who gave you tasks relating to specific locations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In late 1995, when I came back from Rwanda and was asked to look at some grave site, I went with Jean-Rene Ruez and team 6, who were looking for information in -- in Republika Srpska on mass graves and things like that, and interviewing people, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at page 8 of your report, if we can have it shown, that's P1071, the document we see on our screens. We are interested in paragraph 2, where you say: "In the course of a subsequent investigation, on the 29th of May 1996, through the mediation of Jean-Rene Ruez, a grave site was uncovered in Cerska." Can you find that at all?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was discovered at that time, yes, what they thought was a grave, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what sort of a relationship you had as chief anthropologist with the head of investigations, Jean-Rene Ruez, in relation to the Cerska site? What was it that you did in the process of exhumations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, they were not exhumations. He was never -- he never came to a site when we did exhumations. That was done in 1996. It was more an exploratory visit to see if we could find the graves. In fact, we drove up and down that road to Cerska and we never discovered the site of the grave. It was discovered after a time that I had not been there. So I never saw that particular grave until I went to do the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, you were on your feet, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Because of problems with the right page of the document but now we have the right one on the screen. Judge Nyambe has a question for Mr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Haglund, I wonder if you can assist to clarify this. At page 21, no, at line 21, page 36, you have stated that it was discovered after a time that I had not been there. What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently, team 6 knew that there was a grave in that area, but the -- apparently the individual that told them where it was wasn't able to tell them the exact place, and so it had to be somewhere on that road between where the road left the highway and several kilometres up the mountain side where the village of Cerska was. But driving up and down the road, it was -- the grave was not found at the time that I was there. We did not recognise the area where the grave was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, perhaps my question wasn't clear enough. To what extent did you co-operate with Ruez in the course of exhumations and examinations of exhumed bodies and artifacts? Let me be quite precise. I wasn't interested in your personal relationship but your professional relationship. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He had nothing to do with the exhumations or the autopsies or the protocols that went into them and the work that I did and the team members that I had. He was never around and it was my area to make final decisions on and I did that with my -- the people that worked with me, the forensic scientists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the last sentence of paragraph 3, it reads: "These investigations were carried out by experts from Physicians for Human Rights and the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia under the auspices of the ICTY." Can you tell me which investigations are you referring to here in relation to these two institutions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was for the -- there was one forensic evidence individual who collected evidence at our scenes, and there was a photographer, I think from Belgium, might have been from the Netherlands, that took some of our photographs for us. There were only a few, maybe one more, I can't recall this right off-hand, that was on -- that worked with our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in order to understand your answer correctly, this photographer and the other people you are referring to, they worked for the Physicians for Human Rights; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they worked -- they probably were paid by the -- by ICTY or donated by the government, whichever country they came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But again, I think Mr. Tolimir were asking you about the relation between the organisation Physicians for Human Rights and the ICTY, indeed, in my understanding this sentence in your report is not quite clear, "The investigations were carried out by experts from Physicians for Human Rights and International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The interrelation between these two entities and your relation to these people, this is of interest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The Physicians for Human Rights, of course, accepted the invitation to have experts sent. We determined for the most part the experts. They paid for that part, a subsistence allowance while they were there, and then they would communicate if there was any problems or anything that they needed. They -- to my knowledge, they may have requested maybe things done by the Tribunal that they couldn't afford to do or something. I don't know really. But as far as help and experts, as far as members of the team, for the most part that was a Physicians for Human Rights obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were these experts of Physicians for Human Rights normal members of your team which you headed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there never had been a team like this put together before, an international team, so I'd worked with some of the individuals in Croatia in 1993, from Argentina mostly and Latin America, and got to know them, and that was a human rights project also, working for the commission that came in to look at the Vukovar situation and other possible problems with the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? My question was: Was their relation to you the same as of the other members of the team to you, as the head of this group of experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was the head of them. They sent them to me, the Physicians for Human Rights sent the experts as far as the anthropology and archaeology and the majority at the scene were -- they sent them to me at my request. I requested them, particular individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And during that time they worked in this team, they had only obligations for the team and to you but not any obligation for reporting to Physicians for Human Rights or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They got the task only from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I have this question for Mr. Haglund: What sort of authority did the Physicians for Human Rights have as opposed to the authorities vested with the ICTY staff in relation to the exhumations conducted before the bodies and artifacts were, in fact, exhumed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Are you asking what relationship? I'm not quite certain. Could you clarify that a bit? I'm -- it's probably me but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you clarify this for me: You state in your report, when talking about the Physicians for Human Rights -- well, without going into greater detail, what sort of an organisation it was? That's to say, you don't specify in great detail what sort of powers the Physicians for Human Rights had as an organisation, and you as an anthropologist. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, the forensic programme was just one part of PHR's work. They were the ones that originally put together the -- it's the -- the extra legal arbitration and summary of executions that was in 1991, that was a manual suggesting the best things to do and what you could do when you're doing exhumations, and the United Nations had later adopted that. They also worked on terror and they wrote a very famous publication on that which they got the Nobel Prize for. They worked in different countries to assist families who were searching for missing individuals. They have a very -- very many human rights subjects that they deal with. The forensics was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 39, lines 1 through 13, of the transcript, you said that the Tribunal was asked to supply certain things, perhaps this was misinterpretation, but which court of law did you have in mind there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Mostly probably ICTY, I imagine. I'm not quite sure what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And which particular body of the ICTY did you have in mind? Was it the Chambers, the OTP, or any other structure within the ICTY such as the Registry? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think it was mostly doing financial things, it was probably with the Registry. I believe it was mostly to do with financial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The request that they supply them with certain things that you referred to on page 39 of today's transcript, did it have to do with moneys, with funds?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, it had to do with the use of the funds and, for instance, one of them was -- I had specific reference books I wanted to have at the sites -- I mean at the -- where we were working, usually in the lab -- in the autopsy area, and so they would order things for us that we requested or not. One of the things, when we first set up -- okay, I think that's -- so it would be maybe things like that. I wasn't really in touch with their interactions with -- with ICTY except it was something like the books I wanted. Otherwise, I -- as long as we got the resources that we needed to do our work, then that didn't matter to me. And then they may have shared some kind of power over the funding, it may have been shared amongst the Tribunal and Physicians for Human Rights. It wasn't that way in -- in Rwanda. They'd had received the money to themself, but I'm not really sure about the financial things that went on and those kinds of administrative things that went on between Physicians for Human Rights and the Tribunal. I just honestly don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that you did not have, as part of your team, these Physicians for Human Rights, and that they did not receive their tasks as to what they were supposed to do from you but, rather, from the ICTY, to whom they were related? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, no. That's wrong. As I've said before, they worked for me, as far as the decisions that were made once we got to a site and started doing the work. They did not work for ICTY. They were actually sent there by Physicians for Human Rights, and I was the person in charge of them. The major direction I received from ICTY or the major information I received from ICTY were locations of graves, and then from there on, then we did what we needed to do in regard to the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What we can see here is that they had this special channel with the ICTY or so it transpires from your answers, that it wasn't through you that they would exercise their rights and obligations. Is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Are you saying that Physicians for Human Rights had to check with ICTY to -- I'm not quite sure where that's going. As a human rights group, they were not going to take any orders from anybody that would interrupt or be against their charter for what they did as far as human rights were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your -- in one of your replies a little earlier you said that they had certain financial problems and that they dealt with them via the Tribunal, and that's why I asked you what Tribunal that was. So did they resolve these matters through you by way of your mediation or did they have direct contact with the ICTY? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They would have dealt with ICTY, not with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that Physicians for Human Rights had direct contacts with the International Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia rather than going through you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have received many answers in that respect from the witness. He made it very clear that the administrative matters were dealt between the entities and not with him, and the work itself was managed by the witness. I think we are in a circle at the moment. You should try to go ahead with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I felt that these questions were relevant, and I have not really received the answer because I never really got an answer as to the delineation between the jurisdiction or the powers or the work that was being done by the Physicians for Human Rights and the ICTY. But I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, witness, could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, when you say -- when you mention co-operation with the ICTY, what part of the ICTY did you have most co-operation with? Was it with the OTP, with the Office of the Prosecutor, or Jean-Rene Ruez or some other bodies of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It would be the Office of the Prosecutor, the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It was important to clear this up for the transcript. During exhumations, did you work together with Mr. Peter McCloskey, for instance, who at the time, as we know, was a legal adviser in Mr. Jean Ruez's team?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I didn't know who he was. No, I had not met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have a foundation for the facts that Mr. McCloskey was even employed with the ICTY at the time of the exhumations in 1996? I mean, he's assuming facts not in evidence, he's misstating what the facts are. If he wants to ask questions about it, that's fine. But he's misstating things repeatedly, suggesting that the OTP is somehow different from Jean-Rene Ruez. This kind of confusing misstatements and multi-part questions are not getting us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, would you please now take a look at page 10 of this report that's P1071; and specifically the second paragraph in Serbian, and the third paragraph in the English version, which reads as follows -- could the witness please take a look? Autopsy examinations of victims, that's the second paragraph in Serbian, began on July 31st, 1996, and lasted through August 22nd, 1996. "Autopsies were carried out at a temporary morgue established at a war-damaged clothing factory on the outskirts of the town of Kalesija, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Autopsy examinations were carried out under the direction of Robert Kirschner, director of the international forensic programme of Physicians for Human Rights.
