Finalisation of cause and manner of death, as well as editing of final autopsy reports was facilitated by ICTY legal adviser Peter McCloskey." And it was on the basis of this that I put the question a minute ago when I asked you whether you worked with Mr. Peter McCloskey, and I didn't mean to imply anything by that. Could you please answer my question now?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I did not work with Mr. McCloskey on this issue. Basically what I was stating is that basically because there had been some questions about Dr. Kirschner signing the certificates that Mr. McCloskey facilitated carrying these various autopsy reports from various doctors around the world, and he facilitated by carrying them in a locked brief case and carrying them around to different parts of the world and showing them to doctors and saying is this what you wrote? Is this what you want to be on this cause of death? He was just giving it to them so that they could rethink or whatever they wanted to do in case it was ever questioned that Dr. Kirschner's potential changes would be on those documents. That's my understanding at least of what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But you state here very clearly: "Finalisation of cause and manner of death, as well as editing of final autopsy reports, was facilitated by ICTY legal adviser Peter McCloskey." Am I correct? Is that what it states there in your report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's what it states, but he didn't make any decisions on his own. He facilitated what the pathologists would mean as a change or that it was okay and he facilitated them getting to see those documents. He did not change anything himself. He made sure that the proper information was on there, that the original pathologist who signed that particular report, that their information was there. He facilitated those things. He did not do them himself. It's like you hire a carrier to take something for you, they don't change things that you have, they just deliver it. That's basically what he was doing. He was the delivery person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I wonder if you can also clarify for me the exact procedure as who determined the manner of death and the cause of death? Is it the person who prepared the report or was it Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the individual pathologist that did the reports. That was their report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So then why was it necessary for Mr. McCloskey to go all over the world looking for these experts to finalise the cause of -- and manner of death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was because Dr. Kirschner had been blamed for changing some of the causes of death, and it was necessary that that be checked out to make sure that these are the causes of death that the pathologists had on their reports, and in order to maintain chain of custody of this evidence which were autopsy reports, somebody had to accompany those things everywhere they went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: How was Dr. Kirschner blamed for changing some of the causes of death and in what respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically I think I mentioned this previously but when doctors do their reports, they will -- they will itemise the wounds of a person that they had that contributed to the cause of death, like maybe shot to the head, shot to the body, shot to the neck, or whatever. And what Dr. Kirschner I think was trying to do was to try to put that information in a report, you would come out with, for instance, 150 different things to try to tell you about, so he actually tried to categorise this of cause of death and it happens in -- in medical examiners' and corners' offices throughout the United States, also they may change something. The director of the project may change something, but they don't do that without asking the permission of the person that did the autopsy, and apparently Dr. Kirschner may have not asked some of the individuals for their permission before he changed a gunshot to the head, a gunshot to the thorax, three gun shots to the leg, he just put multiple -- multiple gunshot wounds. Otherwise, in order to explain that information in a report, you would have to say this person had one gunshot wound to the head -- there were five people who had a gunshot wound to the head, but if they didn't have a gunshot wound to the neck also, you would also have to say in a separate statement, this person -- three people died of a gunshot to the head and a gunshot wound to the neck, and it would get very, very complicated. He was trying to simplify things that covered what the cause of death was, but he was trying to make is simpler so that it would be easier to put together in a report such as this. I think that's what he was trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just one last question, was Dr. Kirschner one of the doctors working under you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Kirschner, no. He was a pathologist. I am not a pathologist. And as far as the autopsies and that were concerned, the pathologists, basically I did not interfere with them only to provide support and the equipment and that that they may have needed and supplies and supply them with the anthropologists, but the autopsy is a matter of the pathologists, not the anthropologists or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please define for us the term "cause and manner of death"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It varies, the manner of death is a category in which deaths are placed. It's a general category. In the United States, and that's the -- what I use, deaths are either caused by natural causes, they can be caused by suicide, they can be caused by accident, they can cause by homicide, or they may be undetermined. That's the manner of death. It's a collective category -- very simplified categories that you put causes of death into. And then if the -- then the cause of death is the actual injury that participated the death of the individual, so if it was a gunshot wound or stab wound or blunt trauma or being run over intentionally by somebody in an automobile, that would be homicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you've explained the difference between manner of death as opposed to cause of death, could you tell us why it was necessary for someone to do an overview of this - and a person who is not a pathologist or an expert - and that person would then have the final word in the report, because you say here that he facilitated and assisted a lot in finalisation of cause and manner of death. Thank you. So you're speaking here very directly about conclusions drawn. Thank you. A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's a confusing. We can't tell from the question who he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you talking about Dr. Kirschner?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please take a look at the last sentence that I quoted a little earlier on page 10, that we have before us on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just very simple question, were you referring to Dr. Kirschner or to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I'm not referring to anyone specifically. I'm just quoting from this report prepared by Mr. Haglund and that's in the last sentence of this paragraph where it says, "Finalisation of cause and manner of death, as well as editing of final autopsy reports, was facilitated by legal adviser Peter McCloskey." He says very specifically there who helped in the drawing of these conclusions and how. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to stop you at this point in time. If you look at the answer, Dr. Haglund has explained very well the role of Mr. McCloskey. You were asking now, this line 8 and the following on page 49: "Now that you have explained the difference between manner of death as opposed to cause of death, could you tell us why it was necessary for someone to do an overview of this - and the person who is not a pathologist or an expert - and that person would then have the final word in the report..." and so on and so on. Now you are referring to Mr. McCloskey. It was very clear from the explanation of the witness that Mr. McCloskey didn't have anything to do with finalisation of these reports, summarising, and having the final word in the report. This is really a misstatement. Please carry on and bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would now like to refer the witness to paragraph 2 in Serbian, paragraph 3 in English, and specifically the last sentence. Could he just tell me whom he was referring to here where he said that that person helped in the finalisation of cause and manner of death as well as editing of final autopsy reports? Thank you. So who was it who helped in the finalisation? Was it Dr. Kirschner or somebody else? Could you please tell us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Dr. Kirschner was out of the picture. The individual pathologists were the ones that made these changes. I'm not sure what else you ask, I'm sorry. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My apologies if I was imprecise. Now I will ask you very directly: Whom are you referring to in this last sentence where you say that that person was of great assistance in the finalisation of cause and manner of death as well as editing of final autopsy reports? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: What is the -- actually, the paragraph we are looking at? I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is in fact the third paragraph, the last sentence. You are dealing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The [overlapping speakers] preparation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are dealing long time already now with, but Mr. Tolimir, I don't find the words "a person who was of great assistance." It is not in this sentence. If you are referring to this sentence -- the last sentence, with the -- which starts with, "Finalisation of cause and manner of death," then you should quote correctly. Rephrase your question and carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you use the word "help" in the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Facilitate in English or in our language.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I don't have "help" in there, I have "facilitate." "Facilitate" just implies support in making something happen. And that he didn't make the things happen, he just facilitated that other people could make decisions, not him. He just brought papers to them so that they could look at them, hold them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why, then, is it not stated in so many words in the report? Could you tell us, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think it's adequately stated. I don't know how else I would put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your answer, could you please define for us the phrase "editing of final autopsy reports?" What exactly does that mean? Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: When the pathologists looked at their causes of death, if there was a change that they said needed to be made -- if there was -- many, many of the pathologists, as a cause of death, would put multiple gunshot wounds, okay? And that's the way Dr. Kirschner had changed a few of those autopsies. They wanted to make sure that, if gunshot wound was not the cause of death, how was it stated in their original determination of cause of death? And so if it said, "Gunshot wound," multiple gunshot wounds, then that was just fine, but they would have to edit it if Dr. Kirschner had made a change, and so then the pathologist might say, well, three gunshot wounds to the head or ten gunshot wounds to the head. That's the editing, and the pathologists did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us now, please, once an autopsy report is prepared, who has the authority to make any alterations to the facts or conclusions as contained in the report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, the whole issue we have been talking about is if somebody else makes a change to an autopsy report, and -- and the original pathologist who wrote that autopsy report, in order for that change to be made, they have to confer and talk with the original pathologist and they have to agree on it, and so it's the original pathologist that has the authority to do that. However, sometimes it may be considered that a change might be made so the pathologists talk about it. And if there is a change made and they agree on it they make the change, if not they don't, but the point is that Dr. Kirschner apparently did not ask all the pathologists what changes might be made. So the autopsy reports had to be taken back to the pathologists to confirm that this is the correct thing that they wrote, and if it wasn't, then they edited -- the pathologists would edit or change it to what they had originally put down in their paper. What essentially is being said is the same thing, basically, people died of gunshots wounds, it was just the difference in the number of gunshots wounds and the place of the gunshot wounds versus the term -- a general term of gunshot wounds, multiple gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether Dr. Kirschner destroyed the original reports provided by the pathologists and anthropologists where they stated what the cause of death was, and then, whether he produced a new report? Has that ever been established? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I think that was the point, this particular page, he changed it so we would have to put a different page in there, but all the -- the pathologists had copies of their original reports so they knew what they said, so whether he destroyed things or tossed them away, I'm not really certain about that. These are autopsy pathologists areas, and I'm not the person to be involved with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any pathologist provide a statement to the effect that his findings were altered, as relating to the manner and cause of death? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's something I would not be aware of. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why, then, do you claim that Dr. Kirschner actually changed those reports and findings?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I was informed of that, when this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you mention that in your report, who you were informed by and in what manner, of this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain the use of the term "editing" here? Editing of the conclusions -- editing of the final autopsy report, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Editing, I guess, would be in this context, when I guess, it would be any changes made to that document, if it was made -- if a change was made, it was edited, and that's what the pathologist who originally signed the autopsy reports, if they changed it from what the standing document would be, and if there had been a change made that he wasn't aware of, he would put it back in the wording of his own, and that -- my understanding of editing, that's -- that's what editing is. You change something, you correct spelling, you change wording, you change -- they changed the wording back to what they originally said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now state for the record who normally drafts the autopsy report and who is responsible for the accuracy of information contained therein? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, usually it would -- what happens in an office or that the autopsy report, these were actually pages with areas to -- the protocols that you could answer what was necessary for the autopsy, and that would be -- that information would be passed on to somebody on the computer and they would write down what the doctor said and then the doctor would get a draft of that back and then they would go through it and make sure that everything was what they wanted, and then that would be the -- the document would be then reconfirmed after the editing by the pathologist the first time and make sure that it was everything that the doctor wanted, and then that would be the standing of -- of document. Actually, what we did in the field is that they wrote directly on to the document in their own handwriting what these things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the pathologists drafted autopsy reports and that they are responsible for the information contained in the reports?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we have in e-court P1307? That's the report by the oversight committee established pursuant to request by the OTP and which was convened in San Antonio from the 14th to 19th of November 1997? Thank you. We have it on the screens. This is the membership of the committee. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what were the reasons to convene this oversight committee of anthropologists and pathologists? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It was a -- the endeavour was to make sure that the process of what Dr. Kirschner did was right or wrong and what should be done about it, and there were complaints against myself, and they were -- they examined those complaints on the basis of whether these complaints had anything to do with the quality of the forensic information that the team had given. Some three or four of the team had complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us what were the criteria to choose the anthropologists and pathologists that participated in the work of this oversight committee?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The choice of those was made by ICTY. I did get some calls about whether I knew some of these people and if I knew them they thought that any of these -- if I was, you know, friendly with these people that they shouldn't have them on the committee, and I'd say, well -- they would say, "What about this anthropologist?" And I say, "No, I -- he's a very good friend of mine." And they say, "Well, we can't use him." And I said, "Well, yeah, don't." I mean -- so they wanted to get people that, you know, were as far from me as dealing with me in that and knowing me and et cetera, the -- so that they would have as people that just didn't work, you know, they evaluated the work and the personal aspect probably couldn't be blamed of being involved in this decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see here on the screen the list of the members of the oversight committee. You can see that the first five individuals hail from North America, four from United States, where you are also from, and the fifth is from Canada. Then we can see a little further below, that there were two members from the UK. However, the two members from the UK were not present and did not sign any of the findings. So my question for you is as follows: Do you know what was the reason that those two members from United Kingdom did not participate in the work of the oversight committee? And why did they not sign the report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I have nothing to do with the -- this report and how it was put together and who chose who and what. I haven't -- that is, I am separate from that. I was the person being looked at as an investigated basically, and I have no power over this -- this and why people didn't -- the question is a good question but it's not certainly one to be addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So then can you answer this question: Why is it that the preliminary briefings and later debriefings were performed by the people from the ICTY; Peter McCloskey and Jan Kruszewski?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think that's a question for you to ask ICTY and not myself. It was certainly their evidence to protect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are saying in your question why is it that the preliminary briefings and later debriefings were performed by the people from the ICTY. I don't see anything in this document -- I only see that they were present at the briefing and debriefing. But the briefing and debriefing were performed by the two members? I don't see that. Please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I'm going to reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that present at that meeting were Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Kruszewski while they were not members of the oversight committee? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I do not know. They could have had these -- I mean, one thing they could have done is talked to them over the telephone. They didn't have to be present to get their opinions. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But can we see in your report who participated in the work of the oversight committee?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go on to page 2 of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you read the last paragraph? Especially the part where it says, and I quote: "The entire panel is in agreement that there will be no audio or video taping, nor would any outside parties be present during the interview." My question is as follows: Is it true that during all the interviews performed by the oversight committee, the representatives of ICTY, McCloskey and Kruszewski were present? Are you aware of that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to hear the answer first and then I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was interviewed it was only the panel. I wouldn't be surprised if the group was there to inquire of Dr. McCloskey, not to have him a representative of the committee, but I don't know about that for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just -- I have no problem with the answer. I had forgotten that, of course, that Dr. Haglund had been present, and as to his own personal experience with this panel, that's absolutely appropriate. What I was objecting to is him -- is to continue questions about what this panel is doing that are completely outside the knowledge of this witness, but of course as it has to do with Dr. Haglund being interviewed by the panel, that's absolutely appropriate. So I would withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, I would like Mr. Haglund to take a look at page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that on e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This page mainly lists the objections that were addressed to the work in exhumations and the technical processing of the graves. Can you take a look at the following sentence, in the last paragraph, there was also a potential, if not real conflict, between the UN and Physicians for Human Rights personnel as well as variations on legal opinion for cause and manner of death. My question is as follows: Can you explain what conflict is that and what were the differences in legal opinion for cause and manner of death?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I can answer the first part of the question. The conflict between the UN and PHR means that apparently the UN had found out that Dr. Kirschner had changed, had altered, some autopsy reports and that the individual who had altered them was a person representing PHR. That's the conflict, I would assume. The second part of the question, I don't know if I can address.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this oversight committee in the position to determine or to change the opinion on cause and manner of death? Was anybody able to change that text that was written and determined by the pathologist and anthropologists? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the multi-part of these questions. It's very difficult to follow multi-part questions, especially in this report. So if he could limit it to one at a time, I think it would be much more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think both questions have the same content. It's just a repetition of the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What I meant, Mr. President, was built into the question, determine -- determine something and -- determine or change. Determine is one thing. Change is another. And then he keeps going on and asks the questions in a different way. We are not going to get answers to those when he asks questions like that. It's too difficult for the witness in my view, for any witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, last year we have heard so many questions, in fact, combined questions, of many kinds. This one is a quite simple one and I think this witness is capable to answer this question and to tell us about determining the cause of death and change of the determination of cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I will just make one more observation and then I will sit down, and I -- pardon me, I don't mean to be arguing with you, and I absolutely agree with you that this is an intelligent, capable witness and he can do his best to sort this out, but if we go through the transcript and we see all the questions that have been asked by General Tolimir and the answers, we will not see answers to all the questions. It just is not there. I know these topics, I know the questions, and I know the answers. The witness is not answering all of them. And it's not his fault. And that's just the way it is, that's the way the record reflects. I know this because I know the information. It also is part of my legal culture, these kinds of multi-questions would never be allowed where I come from, it's because the witnesses cannot answer all the questions and I see the record. I can go back for you and show all the questions that are not being answered, and it's no one's fault, it's just in my view you can't throw that many questions at a witness and have him answer it. And later on what happens is when an adversary starts arguing from the record, they pick and choose and they criticise the witness for not answering something, or they pick an answer to part of the question and use it for the other part that was not answered. And that is my final point on that matter, Your Honours, and I understand we agree to disagree, and that you are the Judge, and I won't say anything further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, your principal observation is absolutely fine. Everybody would agree to that, but it is the wrong example you picked up. Therefore, to shorten this discussion, I would like to ask the witness: Was this oversight committee in the position to determine or to change the opinion on cause and manner of death? That was the first question. Please provide us with an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, the next question: Was anybody able to change that text that was written and determined by the pathologists and the anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not without their permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Following up on your last answer to Judge Fluegge's question which was, "No, not without their permission," was anybody able to change the text that was written and the determination by the pathologists and anthropologists with or without their permission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would have to have the permission of the individual that did the work, not that they were the only ones, pathologists would be the ones to change things and without getting the -- their permission, those things should not be changed. They did the autopsy. Other people didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I think I have to just ask you again: Was any pathologist or anthropologist asked and gave permission to change the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The issue is a pathologist's reports. I wouldn't be surprised if Dr. Kirschner talked to some of the pathologists and seeing if they would permit the change. He probably explained why and they probably did, but we had 33 different pathologists that summer, and some had come for -- these are doctors that had very busy -- we picked out the best pathologists we could find, and these people are very busy. If they can get away for two weeks from their regular work, that's hard. Some people could get in longer, but -- and they were only there for a certain time, so all those people weren't available at the time Dr. Kirschner was putting together this report. So he may have slipped his memory or he just didn't ask them, but if they were there he would have probably discussed it with, I would think, but that I do not know. I was not in that part and I wasn't involved with the signing of the certificates, but the people would have -- the bottom line is people would -- anybody else besides the pathologists that wrote that report, they would have to have the permission of the doctor that did it. Did that [Realtime transcript read in error "happen"] help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the last question of the witness was not "did that happen" but "did that help"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, it is not my intention to comment the work of one or the other side of the pathologists or anthropologists or others. I'm only interested in one thing. Is the opinion on the cause and manner of death a legal opinion or an opinion of the medical profession? That is the only thing that I'm interested in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't know if I can answer that question, but I know in the United States that the autopsy report is entered as a -- as evidence based on what they say. The certificates that a doctor signs in the United States are legal documents, the cause of death, and that is put on the death certificate - I know many countries don't have those - but in that sense, it's, I think, a legal -- I believe it's a legal document. So the final resolution of the report, on the cause and manner of death is put on actually a death certificate. That's -- that happens in the United States. So I don't know what it is -- I don't know what these documents are legal or illegal or -- they are not illegal but if they are legal or not, I don't know, in many other countries. And we had people from all over the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I assist again? I think there was a misunderstanding. Mr. Tolimir were asking you, is the opinion on the cause and manner of death a legal opinion or an opinion of the medical profession. He was not talking about documents but the opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know if -- I don't know if it's classified as a legal opinion or not. I really don't know. It's a medical opinion based on facts that they see in the autopsy. It's probably not in that sense a legal document, although it's used in the legal system to determine trials and outcomes of trials, et cetera, but that I really don't know the answer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haglund, that's exactly what I wanted to hear from you, whether this has a legal import, that's one thing, and the other thing is whether it also has some legal consequences. So thank you for your explanation. Maybe you could add whether this opinion has some legal consequences in relation to your activities.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. It has consequences. That's why we are here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have page 6? Under "responses" we can find the following and I quote: "There was no clear agreement as to who was responsible for what. We felt that in large part that was due to the fiscal and administrative dichotomy between the UN Tribunal and Physicians for Human Rights, which apparently had never been explained to the working scientists in the field or the morgue." And then it goes further on, saying that there was no clear agreement among you, Dr. Haglund, and Dr. Kirschner. My question is as follows: Since they mention fiscal and administrative problems, can you explain to me and to the Trial Chamber in rather concrete terms, what were those administrative and fiscal problems that influenced your work in the field? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think we've already talked about the fiscal -- if you're talking about financials -- finances, et cetera. The administrative dichotomy, I'm not really sure what they were -- I could only make guesses of what they were. I think you would have to ask these people what they were saying. I can read it just like yourself and I have questions on this document, I don't agree with everything in it, but I did not write it and I do not know the thoughts behind it -- all of them, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation. So can I take your answer to mean -- can the Trial Chamber take your answer to mean that in your opinion the main problems were of the administrative and fiscal nature, or the main problems were the problems of the level of expertise of the persons involved in the work at the locality? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In looking at this, I'd like to readdress the former question if I can a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The relationship between myself and Dr. Kirschner was relatively, I think, known. In the autopsy area, the pathologists were in charge of the pathologists and the other workers that worked for them, be they anthropologists or autopsy technicians or whatever. So in the lab they did know that the pathologists were in charge. However, Dr. Kirschner was absent a great deal of the time, as you see this, and so that would -- may be confusing to people who was their boss at that time. And that was part of the pathology things. So this confusing because often times you were -- when one person left, when Kirschner would leave then he might leave somebody else in charge, but then that person would leave and leave somebody else in charge so that continuance of -- may not have always been obvious to people who came in new and then didn't understand. So -- between myself and Dr. Kirschner, I just looked at him as a pathologist of -- and I knew that that was his area of expertise, and that the individual pathologists, that that was their area of expertise. That was not mine, and so ... does that help? Or does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will see if that helped. We have to continue after the second break. We adjourn now and will resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For witness's travelling purposes we were asked to state if we are going to finish cross-examination today. I believe that we will, in order to accommodate these requirements, we will withdraw some of the planned questions. That's the position of the Defence. Can we have P1307, page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Again, we are discussing the report made in San Antonio --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir could you please repeat the number of the page. The interpreters didn't catch the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wanted to have page 9 of P1307, which is the San Antonio report and we have it on our screens now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have the questions listed here that were put to all the participants in this meeting of the oversight body. And I'm interested in the questions under 9 and 10. I'm quoting: "To whom was authority delegated in the absence of Dr. Haglund?" And 10: "To whom was authority delegated in the absence of Dr. Kirschner?" Can you please answer these questions for us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In my absence from an exhumation Jose Pablo would be the person taking my place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is referring to Mr. Baraybar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And as to Dr. Kirschner, he was supposed to assign someone when he left to take over his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who it was supposed to be? If not, thank you anyhow.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: There were various people, depending upon who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gallagher also participated in the work of this committee. Do you know her?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: She is not a doctor. I think she has a master's.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 5 shown in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sorry for misquoting her title. But you do know the person, that's the only thing I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, yes, that was the problem. The witness wanted to answer your question but you were in discussions with your legal adviser, so we should give the floor to the witness so he can answer the question if Ms. Gallagher also participated in the work of this committee. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, she was one of the persons interviewed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me quote some of her words. Dorothy Gallagher saw problems in the field and in the lab. She stated that Dr. Kirschner changed autopsy reports and instructed her to do so while processing the reports. In the field, Dr. Haglund dictated too much speed in exhumation. The result was commingling and failure to associate body parts. Are you familiar with this statement of hers?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I see it, yes. I'm familiar with the statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you try at a later stage in the morgue to associate various body parts in order to remedy the problem referred to herein by Dr. Gallagher? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That was her perception of a problem, so yes, we would always try to -- to incorporate partial parts of bodies and skeletons and broken bones as much as we could. I don't agree with her statement, and neither did the majority of the rest of the crew, but there were about four, I think, comments that were questioning me, and this is one of them. I don't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the oversight committee establish that Dr. Kirschner modified autopsy reports and advised Dr. Gallagher to do the same? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I was not aware of him advising Dr. Gallagher to -- not -- Dorothy, Ms. Gallagher, thank you so much, to change things. I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But did she make the statement as I've read it in item 13?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I see the same statement you do. It's attributed to her. I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at item 14. Can we have your comments on what the Chilean anthropologist, David Del Pino said, and I'm quoting: "Operations were halted when Dr. Haglund was away. Clothing was discarded at Haglund's command, even though some contained identification."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: We have it -- okay. Have two separate questions. Well, things certainly didn't halt if I left Jose Pablo Baraybar in charge when I was gone. And so that's -- that's his perception. He was a very slow, meticulous worker used to doing archaeology work and it didn't sometimes work out with what we were doing, I think, that was his opinion. And as far as the clothing, you'll see in my report that this is in Pilica, and by that time I realised a return of clothing by the Bosnians, they would accept clothing when we returned the remains to them, but they didn't want clothing that wasn't associated with the body. And I think this had to do with just a couple trousers and a pair of pants that were separate away from the remains in the grave. And as you can see from my report, that I did -- we did search those for any identification documents, any sort of artifacts, anything that would be in them, all of the pockets were empty, there was nothing there. So I left them in the grave knowing that nothing could be done with them anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 5 -- or rather, I'm sorry, paragraph 5 of the San Antonio report in order for us to see what Dr. Clyde Snow [phoen] stated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see paragraph 5 now, and I'm quoting: "He states that sloppy science was done. He felt at times it was Dr. Haglund versus the UNTAES, U-N-T-A-E-S, and mentioned the many bodies removed in one day. Dr. Snow stated that, in his opinion no more than 20 bodies should have been exhumed in a single day. He felt Dr. Haglund showed very poor judgement and that it was lucky nothing had blown up as a result of the procedures used." Can we have your comments, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, he's a very esteemed forensic anthropologist and at one time was a very good friend of mine, and Dr. Snow is of really -- I don't know if he had any experience with graves with partially decomposed remains and saponified remains where you had complete bodies, but I know he was very good at dealing with skeletal remains and he'd -- working with the Argentinians and South Americans for a long time. I'd like to explain what moves -- when you can remove a body and what sometimes it's -- you have to take -- if you have a skeleton and it's separate bones, you have to clean off every bone, find them, you know, over 25 in each hands, same way with the feet, you got 100 little pieces of bone, that takes meticulous care and time to do that. This was not the -- it was not the situation in the former Yugoslavia, for the primary graves, okay? And that means, once you've cleaned off the surface where bodies are lying, once you've mapped them, which we did with electronic device called a Total Station where an individual could stand with an electronic device and somebody would hold up a staff with the markers on it of how deep it was, they could click off the positions of the bodies - the positions of the bodies we do with the head, the shoulders, where the elbows are, where the hands are, where the hips are, where the knees are, where the end of the feet are -- you could probably do that in two to five minutes, period. But when they were doing the original work in Argentina and Latin America, they didn't have those transits, they didn't have those that -- and they had to measure everything. It would take a very long time to do that so that further slowed down the process for them. It made our process very fast. And the -- we were able to document, take out a complete individual's remains relatively quick. Now, it makes a difference whether it's a pile or they are spread out and when, for instance, when if you're working in a latrine, there is only one anthropologist that probably can get in it or in a well because they are a very small place. If you're working in a place like the Cerska grave where you have the remains spread over a large area you can deploy teams of two anthropologists/archeologists and you can have ten teams in there working at the same time so that makes a difference. So there is a lot of difference in the speed and -- it's not what I want to call it speed, but the efficiency of being able to take out remains dependent upon their condition of the amount of decomposition, of how they were arrayed in the grave, et cetera, so I don't agree with that, but people are entitled to their opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us briefly how many bodies were exhumed from the graves you worked on daily?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: How many bodies were removed? Well, on the first day we would come, none would be removed; on the second day come, none would be removed; on the third day come, we probably maybe have some of -- it got down to the remains or found where some of those are. You have to clean out a big enough area so that you really know who is under what other person, who is on the top of them, who is intermingled with them, if you have partial remains and that, so that's a question you can't answer it, as the -- as the exhumations continue then you have varying rates of -- it depends, it just depends upon if a grave is flooded in the morning or if it's not flooded, you have to -- so that's a question I cannot answer. There is no formula to answering that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if there were separate reports written by anthropologists and pathologists or were they compiled as a single report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They were compiled, the -- the reports of the pathologists would reflect the information that the -- they were collecting for the autopsy and that would be reflected in the autopsy report so they did not write separate reports, and neither did they write separate report -- we would have, let's see, 100 times 450 reports if we did something like that, and that would be a chaotic situation. No, they didn't write separate reports. The pathologists -- the pathologists did but the anthropologists and archeologists did not. They made their notes and that and we put that all in one area if they made notes, but -- which they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who oversaw autopsies as they were being conducted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The pathologist doing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And who supervised the work being done in the morgue?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The pathologists. It should have been Dr. Kirschner all the time but he was gone a lot, so he appointed other people to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now call up page 43 in Serbian and 32 in English? And to save time, let me ask you right away. On this page you're referring to -- we are talking about P1072, corpses of vultures, and you said that they could have been the result of those. Thank you. So can you please explain what sort of problems you had to -- on the sites themselves with regard to vultures or animals on the grave site? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Scavengers is a generic term for animals that would eat or move bones or tissues. There were no vultures involved. On two occasions, probably a neighbourhood dog or possibly some wild canid, it would be a canid with long teeth, moved some bones and -- and that was reconciled the next day and you see that in my report. They didn't remove any bones from the site, to my knowledge, but they did remove some -- they did move some remains that we'd had -- we had tarps -- tarps over and rocks, got under and pulled on something, so you saw the leg maybe sticking out or something like that. But that was the only disruption we had in terms of scavengers. This happened in the evening when the -- they would -- it was guarded but it's dark, and, you know, you don't have everything lit up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at P1071, page 65 in English, and 70 in Serbian. It's a table wherein it is stated that in case Cerska 1801 driver's licence, a map, and military orders were found on the person in the grave site -- on the grave site. Do you know what sort of military orders this involved?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I do not know, but we had a translator at the autopsy -- in the autopsy area that translated that for us that's what it was. I put it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us if the orders and the documents you found were preserved as part of the general documentation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That, I think, probably would have been preserved, I'm not sure. Many of the documents on bodies of the -- the identification documents and that were turned over to the group that was trying to identify these people and trying to match up -- there was another PHR project that started out, a family outreach so they could start making a database with the interviews with the families to see if people had broken arms or broken legs or something at some time and how tall they were and the condition of their teeth was and that, and they took those kinds of documents, most of the documents were identification documents, and but if it was a document like this, I'm sure the ICTY would have gotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The document says that these were military orders. We are very much interested in those because a number of inferences can be made from it. Is there a way of gaining access to these, if you know? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That would be a question to ask ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It would probably be up to those who are guarding the documents. And can you tell us, please, who are the ones charged with guarding all the artifacts retrieved from the graves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In the autopsy building, took one room and had a metal door with big locks attached to it, and then we had particular spaces to put the recovered documents, indication of religion or whatever, and all the things we collect from the body, and they were put in that deposit, and then Mr. Gerns would go through the documents he thought that the Tribunal would use and that would be returned -- that would be taken to the Tribunal, and then the other documents would be released to the families, usually identification documents and letters and pictures of families, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in the maps and military orders. Does it indicate to you, as an expert, that the bodies had not been searched by those who killed them? Had this been the case, the orders and identification papers and the rest would probably have been seized. Is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I have no information on whether bodies were searched, but you can see by the report that many people had a lot of documents on them. They had a lot of -- a lot of things in their pockets and letters and things like that. It appears to me that -- I don't know. All I can tell you is what documents we got. I don't know what other people did before we got the bodies. I just -- the bodies are my friend. I don't know anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you now take a look, the third row from the bottom, where it says Osmo Muminovic, and can you now read out what follows after that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: "Driver's licence, identification, and car."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. "Driver's licence, identification card, military orders."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I am interested in military orders and documents. As far as the Defence is concerned, the cross-examination is finished, and I want to thank you, Mr. Haglund, for the answers that you gave me. I also asked some questions that I, as a layman, was curious about because there was a number of discrepancies found by different committees and it was my natural curiosity to ask what was then the truth. I think it was a normal thing to do. I wish you a safe journey home and a joyous stay in Europe. May God bless you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. McCloskey, your re-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have no questions for Dr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has an additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: At page 75, you state, lines 9 -- starting with lines 9: "Many of the documents on bodies investigation documents, and these were basically saying were turned over to the group that was trying to identify these people and trying to match up..." Do you know which group this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the representative of the Bosnian government that were taking control of the bodies and have done exhumations in their own country, and these were the people that were actually dealing with identifications, so it was basically over to the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination here in this trial. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance and the way you were able to provide us with your knowledge and expertise. Thank you very much again, and we wish you a safe travel home and all the best for your health.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience and your good questions and guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much and now you are free to leave the courtroom and the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have ten minutes left but as there is no -- I think we shouldn't start with the next witness because I would like to issue an oral decision of the Chamber and then there are only a few minutes left. If the witness is still waiting, he should be released. On the 25th of January, the Prosecution filed its urgent Prosecution motion to convert witness number 135 from a viva voce witness to a Rule 92 ter witness. In its response filed in English on the 28th of January, both last week, the accused opposes the motion and requests that the Chamber hear the witness viva voce. As a preliminary matter, the Chamber notes that this witness is scheduled to testify this Wednesday, the 2nd of February, and that means the day after tomorrow, and therefore wonders why the Prosecution has waited so long to make this request. The late timing of which has no doubt led to its urgent status. Turning to the merits, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution's motion, in effect, asks the Chamber to reconsider its 92 bis decision of 7th of July 2010 in which the Chamber denied the Prosecution's motion for the witness's evidence to be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Chamber considers that the Prosecution's current motion contains no new arguments in support of admitting this witness's testimony pursuant to Rule 92 ter, except that admission would be in accordance with the Chamber's guidance to the parties on the 29th of November, in which the Chamber reminded each party of the importance of presenting their case as expeditiously as possible. The Chamber considers that its reasons for preferring to receive Witness 135's evidence viva voce are clearly presented in paragraph 118 of its 92 bis decision of the 7th of July and it will not, therefore, repeat those reasons here. In sum, the Chamber has found that the inconsistencies contained in the proposed evidence constitute an overriding interest in the witness's testimony being heard viva voce. The Chamber, having found that there are no circumstances which would justify reconsideration of its 92 bis decision, therefore, denies the Prosecution's motion. This concludes the Chamber's ruling. And this concludes the hearing of today. We adjourn and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom.
